analysis.one_liner: Lets the IRS resume collecting donor information from politically active tax-exempt nonprofits.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2025 with two Democratic cosponsors and has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee without any action since.
analysis.plain_summary: An appropriations law currently forbids the IRS from using its money to require certain tax-exempt nonprofits — the kind that can pour unlimited money into politics without revealing their donors — to report contributor names and addresses [S2]. This bill would lift that ban for fiscal year 2025, letting the IRS again collect donor information from politically active nonprofits [S2]. The goal is to make it possible to trace who is bankrolling "dark money" political campaigns [S2]. The bill was introduced in the House in March 2025 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and taxpayers gain visibility into who funds political influence campaigns that currently run anonymously. The IRS itself regains a tool for checking whether groups claiming tax-exempt status are primarily political outfits. Small-dollar givers to conventional charities are unaffected; the change targets organizations that spend on politics while enjoying tax exemptions [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals, for fiscal year 2025, the appropriations rider (Section 123 of the 2024 Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Act) that bars the IRS from spending money to bring transparency to the political activity of certain nonprofits.

With the rider lifted, the IRS could again require the affected tax-exempt organizations to report the names and addresses of their contributors, creating a paper trail for political spending that is currently anonymous.
The bill was introduced by Rep. Jason Crow (D-CO) with Rep. Nikema Williams (D-GA) as an original cosponsor, and has two cosponsors in total.

analysis.who_pays: Big individual and corporate donors to politically active nonprofits lose their anonymity with the IRS, and those nonprofits take on reporting and compliance work. Organizations on all sides of politics — unions included in some categories — face the same paperwork. Opponents also argue that government-held donor lists can be leaked or misused, chilling people's willingness to associate politically [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Anonymous political donors and dark-money nonprofits

drawbacks.text: The bill is extremely narrow: it lifts the restriction only for fiscal year 2025, so unless extended it would leave the dark-money disclosure ban back in place after that year.

Collecting donor information at the IRS is not the same as publishing it; the public would get transparency only if the agency later shares or acts on the data, and critics warn that giving the IRS lists of political donors revives old fears of the agency being used against political opponents and could chill lawful political giving.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but limited: the bill restores the IRS's ability to see who funds political nonprofits, which is the first step toward any accountability for dark money, but one fiscal year of authority and no public-disclosure mechanism means the practical gain in this bill alone is modest. The cost falls on anonymous donors and nonprofits doing the paperwork, and the honest objection is the risk of sensitive donor data sitting inside the IRS.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee when introduced and has not moved since; Congress is still in session, so it is waiting in committee.

narrative.text: Rep. Jason Crow (D-CO) introduced the End Dark Money Act in the House on March 31, 2025, joined by Rep. Nikema Williams (D-GA).
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax law, and the committee has taken no further action on it.
The bill has two cosponsors, both Democrats.

The restriction the bill targets was written into the annual spending law as Section 123 of the 2024 Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Act (Public Law 118-47), which stops the IRS from spending money to bring transparency to the political activity of certain nonprofits.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo: anonymous political donors and the dark-money nonprofits they fund keep the protection of the spending rider, and no donor-disclosure authority has been restored.

for.name: Rep. Jason Crow
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let the IRS resume collecting donor information from politically active nonprofits.

for.name: Rep. Nikema Williams
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and has taken no action since.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls have occurred; the sponsor and both cosponsors are Democrats, and donor-disclosure measures have generally split along party lines with most Republican lawmakers backing the rider this bill would repeal.

industries.industry: Dark-money political nonprofits (501(c)(4) and similar tax-exempt groups)
industries.note: These groups currently collect unlimited contributions — including from corporations and wealthy individuals — without naming their donors, and the appropriations rider this bill targets protects that anonymity by keeping the IRS from collecting contributor information. Their business model depends on spending in politics while staying anonymous, so their interest runs against the disclosure the bill would restore.

industries.industry: Wealthy individuals and corporations making anonymous political gifts
industries.note: They would have to identify themselves to the IRS when giving to politically active nonprofits, losing the secrecy that lets them influence elections and policy without a public record.
Most groups not engaged in substantial political activity would face little change, though any expansion of donor reporting adds compliance paperwork and raises privacy concerns for ordinary givers.

analysis.trajectory: With only two cosponsors and no committee action months after introduction, the bill is on the standard path to dying quietly at the end of this Congress. The Ways and Means Committee has not scheduled a hearing or markup, and riders like the one it targets are typically reinserted into each year's spending bills, so repeal would need leadership buy-in that is not in evidence.
